article.title: Congress Dodges a Holiday Shutdown, but Hurricane Victims Are Still Waiting

articles.text:
The Senate on Friday night approved a short-term spending bill that keeps the federal government open through January 30, averting a shutdown that would have begun at midnight. The vote was 60 to 38.

The bill includes $12 billion in disaster aid, far short of the $38 billion that governors in Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas requested after this fall's hurricanes. "Twelve billion dollars is a down payment, not a recovery plan," said Senator Ana Torres, a Democrat from Florida, who voted for the measure while criticizing its size.

The legislation also extends the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program at current funding levels. Advocates had warned that a shutdown would have delayed December food benefits for roughly 42 million people.

Eleven Republicans joined most Democrats to pass the bill. Two Democrats, Senators Paul Grant of Oregon and Lena Brooks of Vermont, voted no, saying the bill should have included an extension of expanded child care subsidies that expire at the end of the year.

Senate Majority Leader John Doe, a Republican, said the bill "keeps the lights on" while negotiators work on full-year funding. Conservatives pushed for steeper cuts. Senator Mary Roe of Utah called the bill "another kick of the can."

The White House said President Mark Ellis would sign the measure on Saturday.

article.title: Senate passes stopgap, sending bill to Ellis hours before shutdown deadline

articles.text:
The Senate passed a stopgap funding measure 60-38 on Friday night, sending it to President Ellis hours before government funding was set to lapse at midnight.

The continuing resolution funds agencies at current levels through Jan. 30 and adds $12 billion for disaster relief. It passed the House on Wednesday 231-196.

Eleven Republicans voted with 49 Democrats and independents to clear the 60-vote threshold. Sens. Paul Grant (D-Ore.) and Lena Brooks (D-Vt.) opposed the bill, along with 36 Republicans.

"This is not the bill any of us would have written, but it keeps the lights on," Majority Leader John Doe (R-Ky.) said on the floor ahead of the vote.

Sen. Mary Roe (R-Utah), who led opposition from the right, said the measure was "another kick of the can that adds to a debt our children will pay" and said she would push for spending caps in January.

The Office of Management and Budget had begun instructing agencies on Thursday to prepare for a possible shutdown. A White House spokesperson said Ellis would sign the bill Saturday morning.

Lawmakers now have ten weeks to agree on full-year appropriations, with border security and defense funding the main sticking points.

article.title: US Senate votes to avert government shutdown

articles.text:
The US Senate has passed a temporary funding bill, averting a government shutdown that would have begun at midnight on Friday.

The measure, which passed by 60 votes to 38, funds the federal government until 30 January. It now goes to President Mark Ellis, who is expected to sign it on Saturday.

A shutdown would have forced hundreds of thousands of federal workers to stay home without pay over the Thanksgiving period, and could have disrupted air travel during one of the busiest weeks of the year.

The bill includes $12bn (£9.5bn) in aid for areas hit by hurricanes this autumn. Democrats in affected states said the sum was inadequate.

The vote followed weeks of stalled talks over a full-year budget, with Republicans demanding more money for border security and Democrats opposing cuts to social programmes.

Congress must now reach a longer-term deal before the new deadline at the end of January.

article.title: Senate punts on spending fight again as conservatives slam 'kick the can' stopgap

articles.text:
Senate lawmakers voted 60-38 Friday night to approve yet another stopgap spending bill, pushing the fight over federal spending into the new year as conservatives warned Washington was once again avoiding hard choices.

The continuing resolution keeps the government funded at current levels through Jan. 30. It drew support from 11 Republicans, while 36 Republicans voted against it.

"Another kick of the can that adds to a debt our children will pay," Sen. Mary Roe, R-Utah, said in a floor speech. Roe and other fiscal hawks want binding spending caps attached to any full-year deal.

The national debt passed $38 trillion this fall, according to Treasury Department data.

Senate Majority Leader John Doe, R-Ky., defended the measure, saying a shutdown during the holidays "would have hurt millions of families."

The bill includes $12 billion in disaster relief but no new money for border security, a priority for many Republicans, who argue the southern border remains under strain. Democrats blocked an amendment from Sen. Rick Hale, R-Texas, that would have added $4 billion for border enforcement.

President Ellis is expected to sign the bill Saturday.
Republicans had leverage and gave it away again.
